protocol.question: Does DeepSeek V4 Flash REAP-150B on colibri give better answers than Qwen3.8-27B on llama.cpp for Hermes-style work?
protocol.messages: One user message = the prompt text. No system prompt, no tools. Identical bytes for both models.
protocol.thinking: OFF for the head-to-head on both sides = the production default of each server: llama-server-active runs --jinja --reasoning off (Qwen3.8 template appends an empty <think></think>), colibri's DeepSeek V4 gateway renders the non-thinking '</think>' prefix unless the request sends enable_thinking/reasoning_effort or the server has COLI_THINK=1. The colibri client sends enable_thinking=false explicitly; the llama client sends nothing (server default) and records any reasoning_content anyway.
protocol.budget: Per-prompt max_tokens, identical for both models: math = the context ceiling of each prompt (7808-8000), code 4096, factual/O2/O3 2048, O1 3072. Every budget + prompt fits colibri's --ctx 8192 (the DSV4 engine would otherwise clamp max_tokens to ctx - prompt and the budgets would differ; the colibri client records ctx_clamped to prove it did not). Calibration (qwen-greedy + qwen-hermes seed 1, all 12 prompts, 2026-10-15): 0 of 24 answers hit max_tokens; longest fraction of budget 0.79 (M3 greedy 6267). A prompt marked budget_at_ceiling cannot get a larger budget in this deployment: an answer truncated there is scored as written, for either model, and listed; on any other prompt a Qwen truncation fails the gate (the budget must be raised).
protocol.order: 1. All Qwen arms (qwen-hermes x3, qwen-greedy; qwen-think optional) run first, with Hermes up. 2. Gate: no head-to-head Qwen response may end with finish_reason=length (else that prompt's budget is wrong). 3. The REAP GPU window; the colibri client estimates each prompt's length from the Qwen results.

reap.server: colibri d0e19de2 at shadowfax:/tmp/cw/r6-pr2, :8090, model deepseek-v4-colibri
reap.decoding: greedy (temperature 0 sent; the DSV4 serve engine is greedy anyway)
reap.order: ascending priority. A prompt starts only if its EXPECTED time fits the soft budget (expected tokens = min(max_tokens, 1.5 x r x Qwen's longest head-to-head completion), r = REAP/Qwen length ratio observed so far, clamped 0.5-2). Answers are never cut by the soft budget. A hard stop aborts an in-flight answer (status aborted_window: left out of both models' totals).

qwen-hermes.decoding: Hermes production sampling: temperature 0.7, top_p 0.95, top_k 20, min_p 0, presence_penalty 0.5, repeat_penalty 1.0

qwen-greedy.decoding: temperature 0, top_k 1, presence_penalty 0, repeat_penalty 1 (pure argmax, like colibri, which rejects token penalties)

protocol.loop_guard: Greedy arms only (reap, qwen-greedy): if the last >= 3000 characters of a channel are one exact block of 20-2000 characters repeated >= 5 times, the client closes the stream and records finish_reason loop_abort. Graded exactly like finish_reason=length (scored as written, flagged truncated). Sampled arms only record the detection and keep going.
protocol.missing: status error / incomplete / aborted_window / skipped_budget = no answer: left out of BOTH models' totals for that prompt (paired comparison), listed in the report, re-run when there is time.

prompts.title: Strings over {A,B,C}: no AA, contains BC
prompts.prompt:
How many strings of length 10 over the alphabet {A, B, C} satisfy both of the following conditions?
1. No two A's are adjacent (the string never contains "AA").
2. The string contains "BC" as a contiguous substring at least once.

Show your reasoning step by step, then end your response with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <integer>`.
prompts.solution: Complement inside the no-AA set. No-AA strings: a_n = 2a_{n-1} + 2a_{n-2}, a_1 = 3, a_2 = 8 -> 22, 60, 164, 448, 1224, 3344, 9136, a_10 = 24960. No-AA and no-BC: track the last letter (x = ends A, y = ends B, z = ends C); A may follow B or C, B may follow anything, C may follow A or C: x' = y + z, y' = x + y + z, z' = x + z. From (1,1,1) at n = 1: (2,3,2), (5,7,4), (11,16,9), (25,36,20), (56,81,45), (126,182,101), (283,409,227), (636,919,510), (1429,2065,1146) -> 4640 at n = 10. Answer 24960 - 4640 = 20320 (brute force over 3^10 agrees).

grading.note: compare the integer on the last ANSWER: line

prompts.title: next_cron_times: 5-field cron expression evaluator
prompts.prompt:
Write a Python 3 function

    def next_cron_times(expr: str, start: datetime.datetime, n: int) -> list[datetime.datetime]

that returns, in increasing order, the n earliest times strictly after `start` that match the cron expression `expr`.

Expression format:
- Exactly five fields separated by one or more whitespace characters: minute (0-59), hour (0-23), day-of-month (1-31), month (1-12), day-of-week (0-7; 0 and 7 both mean Sunday, 1 = Monday, ..., 6 = Saturday).
- Each field is a comma-separated list of one or more items. An item is `*` (every value of the field; for day-of-week that is 0-6), `N` (one value), `A-B` (A through B inclusive, A <= B), or `*/S` or `A-B/S` (every S-th value of `*` or of A-B, starting at its first value, S >= 1). A step is only allowed after `*` or a range. There are no month or weekday names and no `?`, `L`, `W` or `#`.
- Day rule: a day field counts as restricted unless it is exactly `*`. If day-of-month and day-of-week are both restricted, a date matches when EITHER of them matches; if only one is restricted, only that one is used; if neither is, every date matches.

Behaviour:
- `start` and the results are naive datetimes. Results have second == 0 and microsecond == 0 and must be later than `start` (a slot equal to `start`, or earlier in the same minute, does not count).
- Raise ValueError for any malformed expression: wrong number of fields, empty item, non-integer, value out of range, A > B, step 0, or a step after a single value.
- Raise ValueError if fewer than n matching times exist within 3000 days after `start` (for example "0 0 30 2 *").
- n >= 1. Use only the standard library. Scanning 3000 days must take at most a few seconds.

Respond with exactly one ```python code block containing the complete solution (imports included) and nothing else.

"""Tiny dependency-free test runner shared by the hidden tests.

The grader copies this file, the test file and the model's code (as solution.py)
into a fresh temp dir and runs `python3 -I <test file>`. Output: one JSON line.
"""
import json
import signal
import sys
import traceback


class _Timeout(Exception):
    pass


def _alarm(signum, frame):
    raise _Timeout()


def run(tests, per_test_s=20):
    signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, _alarm)
    results = []
    for i, (name, fn) in enumerate(tests):
        if i:  # cumulative progress line: if the outer timeout kills us, the grader keeps these counts
            print(json.dumps({"passed": sum(r["ok"] for r in results), "total": len(tests),
                              "partial": True, "results": results}), flush=True)
        signal.alarm(per_test_s)
        try:
            fn()
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": True})
        except _Timeout:
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": False, "error": f"timeout >{per_test_s}s"})
        except BaseException as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - a test failure of any kind
            tb = traceback.format_exception_only(type(e), e)[-1].strip()
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": False, "error": tb[:300]})
        finally:
            signal.alarm(0)
    passed = sum(r["ok"] for r in results)
    print(json.dumps({"passed": passed, "total": len(results), "results": results}))


def raises(exc, fn, *args):
    try:
        fn(*args)
    except exc:
        return
    except BaseException as e:  # wrong exception type
        raise AssertionError(f"expected {exc.__name__}, got {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    raise AssertionError(f"expected {exc.__name__}, nothing raised")

prompts.title: Agent plan: PostgreSQL disk filling while data is flat
prompts.prompt:
You are an operations agent with a sudo shell on an Ubuntu 24.04 VM that runs PostgreSQL 16 (Ubuntu packaging, cluster 16/main, systemd unit postgresql@16-main) for a production web application. Monitoring reports that the filesystem holding /var/lib/postgresql is 93% full and has grown by about 2 percentage points per day for the past week, while the application's tables and indexes have not grown noticeably.

Write the step-by-step plan you would execute. For each step give the exact command(s), what you expect to learn, and how the result decides the next step. Constraints: no data loss, no downtime unless unavoidable, and stop to ask a human before any irreversible or risky action (say exactly which ones). Finish with how you would verify the fix and prevent a recurrence. Keep it under 600 words.

rubric.criterion: WAL retention causes, with exact queries
rubric.description: Replication slots: pg_replication_slots (active, restart_lsn, wal_status, retained size via pg_wal_lsn_diff(pg_current_wal_lsn(), restart_lsn)) 1.5 pt; failing archiving: pg_stat_archiver (failed_count, last_failed_wal), archive_mode/archive_command, server log 1.5 pt. Never deletes files in pg_wal by hand or uses pg_resetwal (1 pt, with a human-approval gate for dropping a slot or changing archiving); correct release mechanism: fix the replica/archive target or pg_drop_replication_slot after approval, then CHECKPOINT and confirm WAL is recycled (1 pt). Emergency headroom only from safe sources (old logs, apt cache, journal).
Re-check df, pg_wal size and slot/archiver status; max_slot_wal_keep_size to cap slot retention; alerts on inactive slots / slot lag, archiver failures and disk usage; log rotation.
Commands are runnable as written (sudo -u postgres psql -c ...), human gates named explicitly, under ~600 words.

critical_errors_minus_3: rm/mv of files in pg_wal or pg_xact, or pg_resetwal
VACUUM FULL / REINDEX presented as the fix although data is flat
stopping or restarting production PostgreSQL as a routine step

prompts.title: Spinner {1,2,4}: P(stop exactly at 8)
prompts.prompt:
A spinner lands on 1, 2 or 4 with probabilities 1/2, 1/3 and 1/6 respectively, independently on each spin. Starting from 0, you spin repeatedly and add each result to a running total, stopping as soon as the total is 8 or more. What is the probability that the total is exactly 8 when you stop? Give the answer as a fraction in lowest terms.

Show your reasoning step by step, then end your response with a final line of the form `ANSWER: <fraction>`.
prompts.solution: The process stops at exactly 8 iff the running total ever equals 8. With p(n) = P(total ever equals n): p(0) = 1, p(n) = p(n-1)/2 + p(n-2)/3 + p(n-4)/6 (p(<0) = 0). p1 = 1/2, p2 = 7/12, p3 = 11/24, p4 = 85/144, p5 = 17/32, p6 = 967/1728, p7 = 1843/3456, p8 = 1843/6912 + 967/5184 + 85/864 = (5529 + 3868 + 2040)/20736 = 11437/20736 (20736 = 2^8 3^4; 11437 is odd, digit sum 16: reduced). ~0.5516. Exhaustive enumeration agrees.

grading.note: Fraction equality; decimals alone are wrong

prompts.title: systemd user unit: Restart=on-failure, start limits, linger
prompts.prompt:
A Linux server (Ubuntu 24.04, systemd 255) runs this systemd user unit, `llm-server.service`, for the user alice:

```
[Unit]
Description=Local LLM server
StartLimitIntervalSec=1800
StartLimitBurst=5

[Service]
Type=simple
ExecStart=/opt/llm/bin/server --port 18080
Restart=on-failure
RestartSec=30

[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
```

Answer each question in one to three sentences:
1. The kernel OOM killer kills the server process with SIGKILL. Does systemd restart it, and if so, how soon?
2. Someone runs `kill <pid>` (SIGTERM). The server does not handle the signal and dies from it. Does systemd restart it? Why or why not?
3. alice runs `systemctl --user stop llm-server`. Does systemd restart it?
4. A bad update makes the server segfault a few seconds after every start. Counting the first start, how many times in total will systemd start it before giving up, and what state and result does the unit end up in?
5. After the bug is fixed, which commands get the unit running again immediately?
6. What exactly is needed for this unit to start at boot even if alice never logs in?
7. If the StartLimitIntervalSec=, StartLimitBurst= and RestartSec= lines were all removed, what values would apply (default manager settings)?

reference_answer.answer: Yes. Death by SIGKILL is an unclean signal, so Restart=on-failure restarts it, after RestartSec=30 seconds.
No. For Restart=on-failure, SIGTERM (like SIGHUP, SIGINT, SIGPIPE) counts as a clean termination; only Restart=always (or on-success) restarts after a clean signal.
No. A stop requested via systemctl/systemd is never followed by an automatic restart.

5 starts in total (StartLimitBurst=5 within 1800 s; with RestartSec=30 all fall well inside the window); the 6th start is refused ('Start request repeated too quickly'); the unit is left 'failed' with result 'start-limit-hit'. 1 pt for 5, 1 pt for failed + start-limit-hit.
`systemctl --user reset-failed llm-server` (clears the failed state and the start-limit counter) then `systemctl --user start llm-server`. Waiting out the 30-minute window then starting: 0.5 only.

Enable it in alice's user manager (`systemctl --user enable llm-server`, linked into default.target via WantedBy) AND enable lingering: `loginctl enable-linger alice` (as root/sudo), so user@<uid>.service starts at boot. Linger 1 pt, enable 0.5 pt.
StartLimitIntervalSec=10s and StartLimitBurst=5 (DefaultStartLimitIntervalSec=/DefaultStartLimitBurst= of the manager), RestartSec=100ms. 0.5 each.

critical_errors: claims SIGTERM death triggers a restart under on-failure
claims systemctl stop is followed by a restart
claims linger is unnecessary for a user unit at boot

prompts.sources: systemd.service(5) Restart= table and RestartSec=; systemd.unit(5) StartLimitIntervalSec=/StartLimitBurst=; systemd-system.conf(5) defaults; loginctl(1) enable-linger. All stable since systemd ~230 (2016).

prompts.title: evaluate: integer expressions with ** and C-style / and %
prompts.prompt:
Write a Python 3 function `evaluate(expr: str) -> int` that evaluates an integer arithmetic expression, without using eval, exec, compile or the ast module.
- Tokens: integer literals (one or more ASCII digits; leading zeros are allowed, so "007" is 7), the operators + - * / % ** and parentheses. Whitespace between tokens is ignored. `**` is a single token and has no space inside it.
- Precedence, from highest to lowest: `**` (right-associative: 2**3**2 is 512); unary + and - (prefix, may repeat: --3 is 3); * / % (left-associative); binary + and - (left-associative). As in Python, a unary minus on the left of ** binds more loosely than **, so -2**2 is -4, and the exponent may itself start with a unary operator, so 2**+3 is 8.
- / is integer division truncating toward zero (7/-2 is -3) and % is the matching remainder, whose sign follows the dividend, so that (a/b)*b + a%b == a (for example -7%2 is -1 and 7%-2 is 1).
- 0**0 is 1. A negative exponent raises ValueError. Division or remainder by zero raises ZeroDivisionError. Results are exact Python ints of any size.
- Any malformed input raises ValueError: empty input, an unknown character (such as ., ^ or a letter), unbalanced or empty parentheses, a missing operand, or two numbers in a row ("3 4").

Respond with exactly one ```python code block containing the complete solution (imports included) and nothing else.

grading.note: a forbidden construct scores the task 0 regardless of tests. Detected with ast.parse (parse only, nothing runs): a call whose function is the bare name eval/exec/compile (unless the code defines that name itself) or builtins.X/__builtins__.X; import/from-import of ast; __import__('ast') or importlib.import_module('ast'). re.compile, self.eval, _eval and comments do not count.

    ("mod_both_neg", "(-7)%(-2)", -1),
    ("mod_paren", "(-8)%3", -2),
    ("zero_pow_zero", "0**0", 1),
    ("big_int", "2**100 + 1", 2 ** 100 + 1),
    ("pow_of_unary_exponent", "2**+3", 8),
    ("whitespace", " \t1 +\n2 ", 3),
    ("nested", "((((3))))*-(-(2))", 6),
    ("div_mod_identity", "(-17/5)*5 + (-17%5)", -17),
]

ERRORS = [
    ("empty", ""), ("blank", "   "), ("trailing_op", "1+"), ("leading_binary", "*2"),
    ("unclosed", "(1+2"), ("unopened", "1+2)"), ("empty_parens", "()"), ("adjacent_numbers", "3 4"),
    ("double_binary", "1 + * 2"), ("negative_exponent", "2 ** -1"), ("float", "1.5"), ("caret", "2 ^ 3"),
    ("letters", "abc"), ("spaced_pow", "2 * * 3"), ("neg_exp_after_unary", "-2**-2"),
]

ZERO = [("div_zero", "1/0"), ("mod_zero", "5%0"), ("div_zero_expr", "1/(2-2)")]


def _v(s, want):
    def t():
        got = evaluate(s)
        assert type(got) is int and got == want, f"{s!r}: got {got!r}, want {want!r}"
    return t


def _e(s, exc):
    def t():
        raises(exc, evaluate, s)
    return t


TESTS = [(f"value_{n}", _v(s, w)) for n, s, w in VALUES] + \
        [(f"error_{n}", _e(s, ValueError)) for n, s in ERRORS] + \

prompts.title: Explanation: lost update in PostgreSQL and five fixes
prompts.prompt: Explain to a backend developer, using PostgreSQL 16 semantics, how a "lost update" can happen when two requests concurrently run a read-modify-write on the same row (SELECT balance ...; compute the new value in the application; UPDATE ... SET balance = <new value>) under the default isolation level. Show the interleaving step by step. Then explain precisely what happens instead with (a) SELECT ... FOR UPDATE, (b) a single atomic UPDATE ... SET balance = balance - 10, (c) REPEATABLE READ, (d) SERIALIZABLE, and (e) optimistic concurrency control with a version column. For each one, say what the application must do (for example, retry). Keep it under 500 words.

rubric.description: Names READ COMMITTED as the default; both read the same value; T2's UPDATE blocks on T1's row lock until T1 commits, then proceeds and overwrites with its stale application-computed value.
T2's SELECT FOR UPDATE blocks until T1 ends, then returns the newly committed row, so the computation uses fresh data; notes blocking, short transactions, consistent lock order / deadlocks.

T2 waits, then PostgreSQL re-checks the updated row version and applies balance - 10 to the committed value: no lost update even under READ COMMITTED; guard business rules with WHERE balance >= 10 and check the row count.
In PostgreSQL, T2's UPDATE waits for T1 and then fails with 'could not serialize access due to concurrent update' (SQLSTATE 40001); the application must roll back and retry the whole transaction.

Also prevents it (SSI), raising 40001 serialization failures, including for anomalies like write skew that REPEATABLE READ allows; needs a retry loop; may abort transactions that would have been fine.
UPDATE ... SET balance = $new, version = version + 1 WHERE id = $id AND version = $read; 0 rows updated means a conflict: reload and retry or report; no locks held between read and write.
Clear timeline, under ~500 words.

critical_errors_minus_2: READ COMMITTED prevents the lost update
PostgreSQL REPEATABLE READ silently loses the update
the atomic UPDATE still loses updates under READ COMMITTED

prompts.title: Careful writing: incident summary for non-technical stakeholders
prompts.prompt:
Write an incident summary email for non-technical stakeholders (sales, support leads and the CEO) about yesterday's checkout problem.

Facts (all times UTC, 14 October 2026):
- 09:12: a settings change to the payment service was released. It mistakenly lowered the number of simultaneous connections the service may open to its database from 200 to 20 (a typo; the intended value was 120).
- 09:15: failed checkouts rose from 0.2% to 38% of attempts.
- 09:31: an automated alert paged the engineer on duty (the alert only fired after 15 minutes above 10% failures).
- 09:44: the change was reversed. 09:52: checkout failures were back to normal.
- About 4,100 customers had a checkout fail; 2,650 of them retried successfully within the hour; about 1,450 did not retry. Support received 212 tickets.
- No card was charged twice and no payment data was exposed (confirmed by the payments team).
- Not yet known: how many of the ~1,450 customers who did not retry were lost for good. The analytics team will report by 17 October.
- Follow-ups: (1) automatic checks that reject this setting below 50 before release - owner Priya, due 21 October; (2) make the alert fire after 3 minutes instead of 15 - owner Marcus, due 16 October; (3) email the customers who did not retry, with a 10% discount code - owner Dana (support), due 18 October.

Requirements:
- A subject line, then a body of at most 200 words.
- Plain language. Do not use any of these words or phrases: connection pool, config, configuration, deploy, deployed, deployment, rollback, rolled back, on-call.
- State how long customers were affected.
- Include all three follow-ups with their owners and due dates.
- Say clearly what is not yet known.
- Do not blame any individual, and do not add any fact or number that is not given above.

rubric.description: Impact 09:15-09:52 UTC = 37 minutes on 14 Oct; ~4,100 customers affected; 2,650 retried successfully; ~1,450 did not; 212 tickets; no double charges and no payment data exposed. -0.5 per missing or wrong key fact (floor 0).
Clearly says it is not yet known how many of the ~1,450 were lost for good, with the 17 Oct analytics report.
All three with correct owner and date: checks rejecting values below 50 (Priya, 21 Oct); alert after 3 instead of 15 minutes (Marcus, 16 Oct); discount email to non-retrying customers (Dana, 18 Oct).

The cause is explained without jargon (a mistyped setting limited how many connections the payment system could make to its database). Related words that are not on the banned list (e.g. configured, redeploy) may cost points here, at the judge's discretion; they are listed in auto_checks.related_terms_used.
0.75 if auto_checks.banned_terms_used is empty, else 0 (see banned_term_policy).
0.5 if auto_checks.has_subject.
0.5 if auto_checks.body_words <= 200 (whitespace-separated tokens that contain a letter or digit, in the lines after the subject line).
No individual blamed for the mistake (owners of follow-ups are fine); calm, accountable, apologetic where appropriate.
What happened / impact / what is next, readable by a non-technical reader.

automated_checks.banned_term_policy: A violation is a listed term or a regular inflection of it (plural, -s, -ing; for 'rolled back' also roll/rolls/rolling back; for 'on-call' also 'on call' and 'oncall'; 'roll back'/'roll-back' as a noun = rollback), as a whole word, case-insensitive, with any spacing or hyphenation inside a phrase. Words that only share a root and are not on the list (configure, configured, reconfigured, redeploy, deployable) are not automatic violations; they are reported as related_terms_used for the judge's plain-language score.

prompts.title: shell_split: POSIX-style quoting without shlex
prompts.prompt:
Write a Python 3 function `shell_split(s: str) -> list[str]` that splits a command line into words using the following quoting rules (a subset of POSIX shell quoting). Do not use the shlex module.
- Outside quotes, whitespace (space, tab, carriage return, newline) separates words; a run of whitespace counts as one separator, and leading or trailing whitespace is ignored.
- Outside quotes, a backslash makes the next character literal, whatever it is (including whitespace, a quote, a newline or another backslash): that character is kept and the backslash is dropped.
- Single quotes: every character up to the next single quote is literal, backslashes included.
- Double quotes: every character up to the closing double quote is literal, except that a backslash followed by `"` or `\` produces just that second character. A backslash followed by any other character is kept, together with that character.
- Quoted and unquoted pieces that touch form one word: a'b c'"d" is the single word `ab cd`. A pair of quotes with nothing inside still creates a word, so `a '' b` gives ["a", "", "b"].
- No other character is special: ; | & < > $ ` # * ( ) are ordinary characters.
- Raise ValueError for an unterminated single or double quote, or for a backslash that is the last character of the input.

Respond with exactly one ```python code block containing the complete solution (imports included) and nothing else.

grading.note: expected values equal shlex.split(s). shlex is also blocked at import time. Any import of shlex (found by ast.parse of the code, nothing executed) scores 0, as the prompt forbids it; v1's no_shlex test (1/25 for lazy imports) is gone.

prompts.hidden_tests:
"""Hidden tests for C2 shell_split. Expected values equal shlex.split(s) (posix, no comments).
The shlex module is blocked before the solution is imported (a solution that imports it fails
its tests; grade.py also scores it 0 by a static check)."""
import sys

sys.path.insert(0, ".")
sys.modules["shlex"] = None  # `import shlex` in the solution raises ImportError
from _runner import raises, run  # noqa: E402

try:
    from solution import shell_split
except BaseException as e:
    def shell_split(*a, _e=e):
        raise RuntimeError(f"import failed: {_e!r}")

CASES = [
    ("simple", "ls -la /tmp", ["ls", "-la", "/tmp"]),
    ("runs_of_ws", "  a \t b\n\nc  ", ["a", "b", "c"]),
    ("empty_input", "", []),
    ("only_ws", " \t\n ", []),
    ("single_quotes", "echo 'hello   world'", ["echo", "hello   world"]),
    ("single_quote_backslash_literal", r"printf 'a\nb\'", ["printf", "a\\nb\\"]),
    ("double_quotes", 'say "two words"', ["say", "two words"]),
    ("dq_escaped_quote_and_backslash", r'"a\"b\\c"', ['a"b\\c']),
    ("dq_other_backslash_kept", r'"a\$b\nc"', ["a\\$b\\nc"]),
    ("adjacent_parts_concatenate", "a'b c'\"d\"e", ["ab cde"]),
    ("empty_quotes_alone", "a '' b \"\"", ["a", "", "b", ""]),
    ("empty_quotes_attached", "x''y", ["xy"]),
    ("backslash_space", r"a\ b c", ["a b", "c"]),
    ("backslash_quote_outside", r"\'x\" \\", ["'x\"", "\\"]),
    ("backslash_newline_outside_kept", "a\\\nb", ["a\nb"]),
    ("special_chars_ordinary", "a;b | c&&d > e $HOME #x `y` (z)", ["a;b", "|", "c&&d", ">", "e", "$HOME", "#x", "`y`", "(z)"]),
    ("option_with_quoted_value", '--opt="hello world" -x', ["--opt=hello world", "-x"]),
    ("quote_inside_other_quote", "\"it's\" 'say \"hi\"'", ["it's", 'say "hi"']),
    ("unicode", "café 'naïve x' \"日本\"", ["café", "naïve x", "日本"]),
    ("carriage_return_ws", "a\r\nb", ["a", "b"]),
]

ERRORS = [
    ("unterminated_single", "echo 'oops"),
    ("unterminated_double", 'echo "oops'),
    ("trailing_backslash", "echo \\"),
    ("dq_ends_with_escaped_quote", '"abc\\"'),
]


def _mk(s, want):
    def t():
        got = shell_split(s)
        assert got == want, f"{s!r}: got {got!r}, want {want!r}"
    return t


def _mk_err(s):
    def t():
        raises(ValueError, shell_split, s)
    return t


TESTS = [(f"case_{n}", _mk(s, w)) for n, s, w in CASES] + \
        [(f"error_{n}", _mk_err(s)) for n, s in ERRORS]
# v2: no "no_shlex" test any more. It gave 1/25 to a solution that imports shlex lazily inside the
# function; grade.py now finds any shlex import with ast.parse and scores the task 0 instead.

if __name__ == "__main__":
    run(TESTS)
prompts.test_runner:
"""Tiny dependency-free test runner shared by the hidden tests.

The grader copies this file, the test file and the model's code (as solution.py)
into a fresh temp dir and runs `python3 -I <test file>`. Output: one JSON line.
"""
import json
import signal
import sys
import traceback


class _Timeout(Exception):
    pass


def _alarm(signum, frame):
    raise _Timeout()


def run(tests, per_test_s=20):
    signal.signal(signal.SIGALRM, _alarm)
    results = []
    for i, (name, fn) in enumerate(tests):
        if i:  # cumulative progress line: if the outer timeout kills us, the grader keeps these counts
            print(json.dumps({"passed": sum(r["ok"] for r in results), "total": len(tests),
                              "partial": True, "results": results}), flush=True)
        signal.alarm(per_test_s)
        try:
            fn()
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": True})
        except _Timeout:
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": False, "error": f"timeout >{per_test_s}s"})
        except BaseException as e:  # noqa: BLE001 - a test failure of any kind
            tb = traceback.format_exception_only(type(e), e)[-1].strip()
            results.append({"test": name, "ok": False, "error": tb[:300]})
        finally:
            signal.alarm(0)
    passed = sum(r["ok"] for r in results)
    print(json.dumps({"passed": passed, "total": len(results), "results": results}))


def raises(exc, fn, *args):
    try:
        fn(*args)
    except exc:
        return
    except BaseException as e:  # wrong exception type
        raise AssertionError(f"expected {exc.__name__}, got {type(e).__name__}: {e}")
    raise AssertionError(f"expected {exc.__name__}, nothing raised")

prompts.title: Six-service restart order puzzle (unique solution)
prompts.prompt:
Six services - api, auth, cache, db, proxy and worker - must each be restarted exactly once, one at a time, in positions 1 to 6. The order must satisfy all of these rules:
1. proxy is restarted either first or last.
2. cache is not restarted immediately before or immediately after db.
3. If proxy is restarted first, then worker is restarted last.
4. api and worker are not restarted consecutively (in either order).
5. Exactly two other services are restarted between db and api (db may come before or after api).
6. auth is restarted in an even-numbered position (2nd, 4th or 6th).
Find the only order that satisfies every rule, and explain why no other order works.

Show your reasoning step by step, then end your response with a final line of the form `ANSWER: s1, s2, s3, s4, s5, s6`.
prompts.reference_answer: proxy, api, cache, auth, db, worker
prompts.solution: Case proxy = 6: auth in {2,4}; {db, api} occupy positions 3 apart within 1..5: {1,4} or {2,5}. {1,4}: auth = 2, cache/worker take {3,5}; db = 4 would put cache next to it, so db = 1, api = 4, but then worker (3 or 5) is next to api: impossible. {2,5}: auth = 4, cache/worker take {1,3}; db = 2 is adjacent to both, so db = 5, api = 2, and worker (1 or 3) is next to api: impossible. Case proxy = 1: worker = 6 (rule 3); {db, api} within 2..5 three apart = {2,5}; auth = 4 (2 is taken), cache = 3; cache must not touch db, so db = 5, api = 2. api (2) and worker (6) are not adjacent. Unique: proxy, api, cache, auth, db, worker (brute force over all 720 orders confirms exactly one).

grading.note: compare the ordered list of six names

prompts.title: TCP TIME_WAIT on Linux
prompts.prompt:
Answer each question about TCP on a stock Linux kernel (for example 6.1 or 6.6 LTS) in one to three sentences:
1. Which side of a TCP connection enters the TIME_WAIT state?
2. What are the two reasons TIME_WAIT exists?
3. How long does a socket stay in TIME_WAIT on Linux, and can you shorten that with `net.ipv4.tcp_fin_timeout`?
4. What does `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_reuse` do, and what does it rely on?
5. What happened to `net.ipv4.tcp_tw_recycle`, and why?
6. A web server is restarted and bind() fails with EADDRINUSE because old connections on its port are in TIME_WAIT. Which socket option fixes this, and how does it differ from SO_REUSEPORT?
7. A client opens many short-lived connections to the same server IP and port and runs out of local ports. Give two effective mitigations.

reference_answer.answer: The side that closes first (active close: sends the first FIN). Both sides in a simultaneous close.

(a) Reliable close: if the final ACK is lost the peer retransmits its FIN and the TIME_WAIT side can re-ACK instead of answering with RST. (b) Let delayed duplicate segments of the old connection die out so a new incarnation of the same 4-tuple cannot accept them. 1 pt each.
60 seconds, a compile-time constant (TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN; the RFC's 2*MSL). No: tcp_fin_timeout controls how long an orphaned connection stays in FIN_WAIT_2, not TIME_WAIT. 1 pt each.

Lets the kernel reuse a TIME_WAIT socket's 4-tuple for a NEW OUTGOING connection (connect side only, not incoming) when protocol-safe, relying on TCP timestamps (net.ipv4.tcp_timestamps) to reject old duplicates. 0.5 purpose, 0.5 outgoing-only, 0.5 timestamps.
Removed in Linux 4.12 (2017); it broke clients behind NAT (per-host timestamp checks dropped their SYNs). 0.5 removed, 0.5 NAT reason.

SO_REUSEADDR (set before bind()) lets the listener bind despite TIME_WAIT connections on the port. SO_REUSEPORT lets several sockets bind the same address:port simultaneously, with the kernel load-balancing incoming connections. 1 + 0.5.

Any two of: reuse connections (keep-alive / pooling); tcp_tw_reuse=1 with timestamps; widen net.ipv4.ip_local_port_range; spread over more destination IPs/ports or source IPs; have the server close first. Not credited: lowering tcp_fin_timeout, tcp_tw_recycle. 0.5 each.

critical_errors: says tcp_fin_timeout sets the TIME_WAIT duration

prompts.sources: RFC 793/9293 (TIME-WAIT, 2*MSL); Linux include/net/tcp.h TCP_TIMEWAIT_LEN (60*HZ); Documentation/networking/ip-sysctl.rst (tcp_fin_timeout, tcp_tw_reuse); tcp_tw_recycle removal commit in 4.12; socket(7) SO_REUSEADDR/SO_REUSEPORT.
